DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Introducing an Off-Peak Membership
Pulse Fitness, Commercial Team, August 2026

1. Proposal
We propose introducing an off-peak membership at £29 a month from 1 October 2026, alongside our existing standard membership at £42 a month. Off-peak members would have access before 4 pm on weekdays and all day at weekends, with full access to the gym floor and to classes running in those hours.

2. Background
Pulse operates four clubs with 9,600 standard members. Membership has been flat for 18 months, while two budget gyms have opened within our catchments, both offering memberships at £22 to £25 a month. Our clubs are busy between 5 pm and 8 pm on weekdays, when the gym floor often runs at or near capacity, but quiet during weekday daytimes, when typical utilisation is around 30%.

Access-control data for May to July 2026 show that 31% of our current standard members visit exclusively in what would be the off-peak window, and a further 22% visit mostly off-peak.

3. Market evidence
A survey of 640 non-members living within two miles of our clubs, conducted in June, found that 19% would "definitely" or "probably" join at £29 a month for off-peak access. The most interested groups were retirees, shift workers, parents of school-age children and students.

Four of our six closest competitors already offer an off-peak or daytime membership, priced between £25 and £32.

4. Classes and retention
Retention is the other half of our commercial challenge. Monthly churn among members who attend at least one class a week is 2.1%, against 4.8% among members who do not attend classes. Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week to support the new membership, which should lower churn among off-peak members towards the 2.1% level. The additional classes would cost £18,700 a month across the four clubs in instructor fees.

5. Revenue projection
We expect to recruit 1,200 new off-peak members in the first year, about 300 per club, which is consistent with the survey response and the size of our catchments. At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue. After the cost of the additional classes (£224,400 a year), net additional revenue is £193,200 a year.

Because daytime utilisation is low, the additional members can be accommodated without investment in equipment or space.

6. Operational changes
Access control will be updated so that off-peak members' cards do not open the turnstiles outside their access window. Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm, giving those finishing early shifts or school pick-ups time to train. Members will be able to upgrade to standard membership at any time, and to switch between membership types with one month's notice.

7. Risks
Some standard members may perceive the off-peak price as unfair. We will communicate the change as an extension of choice. Competitor responses are possible; the budget gyms already price below our proposed off-peak rate, so we do not expect a price war.

8. Staff consultation
Club managers and front-of-house teams at all four clubs were consulted in July. Managers supported the proposal, noting that daytime classes are often under-filled and that a daytime membership would help build a regular community at quieter times. Front-of-house staff asked for clear signage and app messaging about access hours, which we will provide before launch.

9. Recommendation
The off-peak membership fills spare daytime capacity, responds to competitor offers and targets clearly identified customer groups. We project net additional revenue of around £193,000 a year and recommend launch on 1 October 2026.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Off-peak members will have weekday access until 5 pm" -- Section 1 defines off-peak access as before 4 pm on weekdays; section 6 says off-peak members have weekday access until 5 pm (also into the busy 5-8 pm period the document says is near capacity). The access window contradicts itself.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "Classes clearly keep members loyal, so we will add six extra daytime classes per club each week" -- The churn difference is correlational: members who choose to attend classes weekly are likely more engaged/committed to begin with (self-selection). It does not show classes cause lower churn, nor that adding classes would bring off-peak churn to 2.1%.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £29 a month, this is £34,800 a month, or £417,600 a year, in new membership revenue." -- The projection counts only new members and ignores downgrades, although the document states 31% of the 9,600 standard members (about 2,976) already visit only off-peak and can switch with one month's notice. If they downgraded, revenue would fall by about £13 x 2,976 = £38,700 a month (about £464,000 a year), more than wiping out the projected gain.

REVIEW:
# Review: Off-Peak Membership Pricing Proposal

The proposal is clearly written, the arithmetic is internally correct, and the operational and staff-consultation sections are useful. But the core financial case leaves out its largest effect. Once that is included, the projected £193,000 gain is likely to become a loss. Several claims in your description are also stronger than the document supports.

## 1. Cannibalisation is missing, and it is likely bigger than the projected gain

Section 2 says 31% of standard members visit only in the off-peak window, and another 22% visit mostly off-peak. The proposal uses this as evidence of spare capacity, but it is really evidence that many existing members would pay less under the new tier.

- 31% of 9,600 is **2,976 members** who could switch from £42 to £29 and lose nothing.
- Each switch costs **£13 a month, or £156 a year**.
- If they all switch, revenue falls by **£464,256 a year**. That is more than the entire £417,600 gross from new members.
- **Break-even:** if about 1,240 members switch (around 42% of the exclusive off-peak group, or 13% of the base), the net gain is gone. This ignores the 2,112 "mostly off-peak" members, some of whom would also switch.

Section 6 makes this easier still by letting members switch tiers with one month's notice. The Risks section discusses whether the price seems unfair, but not the revenue loss. The "upgrade at any time" point in your description works the wrong way here: downgrades are the risk.

**Suggestion:** Add a cannibalisation line to the projection, with scenarios such as 25%, 50% and 100% of exclusive off-peak users switching. Then consider controls: a narrower window, fewer inclusions (for example, a classes add-on), or new-joiner-only availability for an initial period.

## 2. The access window is inconsistent

- Section 1 says access is **before 4 pm**.
- Section 6 says **until 5 pm**.

This matters. 5 pm is when the peak starts (Section 2), so a 5 pm cut-off pushes off-peak members into the busiest period. It also widens the group of existing members who could switch. The 31%/22% figures were measured against "what would be the off-peak window", so the document should say which window was used.

## 3. The revenue projection assumes a full year from every new member

The £417,600 figure treats all 1,200 members as paying for 12 months. In practice:

- **Recruitment is spread over the year.** If sign-ups are roughly even, the average paying base is about 600, giving roughly **£209,000** in first-year gross. That is already below the £224,400 class cost, before any cannibalisation.
- **Churn is ignored.** Even at the optimistic 2.1% monthly rate, about 22% of a cohort leaves within a year. At 4.8%, about 45% leaves.
- **VAT:** if £29 includes VAT, net revenue per member is about £24.17, which cuts gross revenue by a sixth. Please confirm the basis.
- **Other costs** are missing: marketing for launch, access-control and app changes, and signage.

## 4. "Conservative" and "consistent with the survey" are not shown

- The document gives no catchment population, so the reader cannot check that 1,200 members is "well within what the survey implies".
- "Definitely or probably would join" is stated intent. Actual conversion is usually much lower, especially for "probably". A standard discount, such as counting a fraction of "definitely" responses and few "probably" responses, would support the "conservative" claim.
- Respondents were asked about £29 off-peak. The document does not say whether they saw it alongside the £22–25 full-access budget options that compete for the same people.

## 5. The classes-and-retention logic has two problems

- **Correlation, not causation.** Members who attend classes may churn less because they were more engaged to begin with. Adding classes will not necessarily move off-peak members towards 2.1%. The document says "clearly keep members loyal", and your description calls the classes "an investment", but the evidence does not establish this.
- **It conflicts with Section 8.** Managers report that daytime classes are "often under-filled". Adding 24 more daytime classes a week across the estate needs a reason beyond the churn figure. Filling existing classes may get most of the retention benefit at no extra cost.
- **Check the cost.** 24 classes a week is about 104 a month, so £18,700 works out to roughly **£180 per class** in instructor fees. That seems high and is worth confirming.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Weekend capacity:** off-peak includes all day at weekends, but Section 2 only shows that weekday daytimes are quiet. Please give weekend utilisation, or reconsider including weekends. This also affects how many standard members could switch.
- **Competitor reasoning:** "Budget gyms already price below us, so no price war" does not follow. Competitors could respond with their own off-peak tiers. The four of six competitors that already offer off-peak are the more relevant comparison.
- **Spare-capacity evidence:** your description credits the access-control data with showing spare capacity. That point actually rests on the 30% utilisation figure. The access-control data mainly show the cannibalisation exposure.
- **Dates:** the document is dated August 2026 and recommends launching on 1 October 2026. If it is being circulated now, the timeline needs updating.

## Overall

The strategic logic is reasonable: there is spare daytime capacity, competitors offer off-peak tiers, and clear target groups exist. But the financial case is not yet sound. A revised projection should include:

1. Cannibalisation scenarios.
2. A realistic ramp-up and churn.
3. VAT and launch costs.
4. A survey conversion assumption tied to the actual catchment population.

On current figures, the most likely result is a net loss. I would not describe the proposal as low-risk until those numbers are shown.
